In [[algebraic geometry]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''Lefschetz theorem on (1,1)-classes''', named after [[Solomon Lefschetz]], is a classical statement relating holomorphic [[line bundle]]s on a [[compact space|compact]] [[Kähler manifold]] to classes in its integral [[cohomology]]. It is the only case of the [[Hodge conjecture]] which has been proved for all Kähler manifolds.<ref>{{Harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|p=163}}</ref>

== Statement of the theorem ==
Let ''X'' be a compact Kähler manifold. The first [[Chern class]] ''c''<sub>1</sub> gives a map from holomorphic line bundles to {{nowrap|''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''')}}. By [[Hodge theory]], the [[de Rham cohomology]] group ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''C''') decomposes as a direct sum {{nowrap|''H''<sup>0,2</sup>(''X'') &oplus; ''H''<sup>1,1</sup>(''X'') &oplus; ''H''<sup>2,0</sup>(''X'')}}, and it can be proven that the image of ''c''<sub>1</sub> lies in ''H''<sup>1,1</sup>(''X''). The theorem says that the map to {{nowrap|''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''') &cap; ''H''<sup>1,1</sup>(''X'')}} is surjective.

In the special case where ''X'' is a [[projective variety]], holomorphic line bundles are in bijection with linear equivalences class of [[divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisor]]s, and given a divisor ''D'' on ''X'' with associated line bundle ''O(D)'', the class ''c''<sub>1</sub>(''O(D)'') is Poincaré dual to the homology class given by ''D''. Thus, this establishes the usual formulation of the Hodge conjecture for divisors in projective varieties.

== Proof using normal functions ==
Lefschetz's original proof<ref>{{Harvnb|Lefschetz|1924}}</ref> worked on projective surfaces and used normal functions, which were introduced by Poincaré. Suppose that ''C''<sub>''t''</sub> is a pencil of curves on ''X''. Each of these curves has a [[Jacobian variety]] ''JC''<sub>''t''</sub> (if a curve is singular, there is an appropriate generalized Jacobian variety). These can be assembled into a family <math>\mathcal{J}</math>, the Jacobian of the pencil, which comes with a projection map π to the base ''T'' of the pencil. A '''normal function''' is a (holomorphic) section of π.

Fix an embedding of ''X'' in '''P'''<sup>''N''</sup>, and choose a pencil of curves ''C''<sub>''t''</sub> on ''X''.  For a fixed curve Γ on ''X'', the intersection of Γ and ''C''<sub>''t''</sub> is a divisor {{nowrap|''p''<sub>1</sub>(''t'') + ... + ''p''<sub>''d''</sub>(''t'')}} on ''C''<sub>''t''</sub>, where ''d'' is the degree of ''X''. Fix a base point ''p''<sub>0</sub> of the pencil.  Then the divisor {{nowrap|''p''<sub>1</sub>(''t'') + ... + ''p''<sub>''d''</sub>(''t'') &minus; ''dp''<sub>0</sub>}} is a divisor of degree zero, and consequently it determines a class ν<sub>Γ</sub>(''t'') in the Jacobian ''JC''<sub>''t''</sub> for all ''t''. The map from ''t'' to ν<sub>Γ</sub>(''t'') is a normal function. 

[[Henri Poincaré]] proved that for a general pencil of curves, all normal functions arose as ν<sub>Γ</sub>(''t'') for some choice of Γ. Lefschetz proved that any normal function determined a class in ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''') and that the class of ν<sub>Γ</sub> is the fundamental class of Γ. Furthermore, he proved that a class in ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''') is the class of a normal function if and only if it lies in ''H''<sup>1,1</sup>. Together with Poincaré's existence theorem, this proves the theorem on (1,1)-classes.

== Proof using sheaf cohomology ==
Because ''X'' is a complex manifold, it admits an [[exponential sheaf sequence]]<ref>{{Harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|p=37}}</ref>
:<math>0 \to \underline{\mathbf{Z}} \stackrel{2\pi i}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{O}_X \stackrel{\operatorname{exp}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{O}_X^\times \to 0.</math>
Taking [[sheaf cohomology]] of this exact sequence gives maps
:<math>H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X^\times) \stackrel{c_1}{\to} H^2(X, \mathbf{Z}) \stackrel{i_*}{\to} H^2(X, \mathcal{O}_X).</math>
The group {{nowrap|Pic ''X''}} of [[line bundle]]s on ''X'' is isomorphic to <math>H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X^\times)</math>. The first Chern class map is ''c''<sub>1</sub> by definition, so it suffices to show that <math>i_*</math> is zero on {{nowrap|''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''') &cap; ''H''<sup>1,1</sup>(''X'')}}.

Because ''X'' is Kähler, [[Hodge theory]] implies that <math>H^2(X, \mathcal{O}_X) \cong H^{0,2}(X)</math>. However,  <math>i_*</math> factors through the map from ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''') to ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''C'''), and on ''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''C'''), <math>i_*</math> is the restriction of the projection onto ''H''<sup>0,2</sup>(''X''). It follows that it is zero on {{nowrap|''H''<sup>2</sup>(''X'', '''Z''') &cap; ''H''<sup>1,1</sup>(''X'')}}, and consequently that the cycle class map is surjective.<ref>{{Harvnb|Griffiths|Harris|1994|pp=163&ndash;164}}</ref>
